AUTOPSY REPORT
Maison Delorme’s shipping director.
Maison Delorme’s business relationships are confidential.

On behalf of Maison Delorme. After Mercier’s unfortunate incident, I took over the private sales. Henri’s death postpones the sale, that’s all. I was in the library all evening; Mr Doyle is my witness.
He turns his ring with his thumb.
Were you running the sale?
Antoine Brassard — interview
Wine expert.

The twelve bottles on the sale list. One 1961 has a new cork; opened within six months and recorked. The wine inside isn’t 1961, it’s five years old at most. I told Henri at 21.45. His face went white; he said, ‘I’ll go down to the cellar and check them all.’
He raises his eyebrows and drums his fingers on the table.
What did you examine this evening?
My appraisal reports belong to my client.
Yves Caron — interview
The sommelier, for twenty years. Henri trusted him blindly.
Who ran the cellar?

The death was deemed an accident; the sale went ahead two weeks later.
Antoine Brassard was taken into custody and released the next day; the sommelier carried on working.

The blow came from behind, single and round-based; there is blood on the base of the broken magnum. A bottle falling from a rack doesn’t strike like that.

The expert exposed the forgery at 21.45; the sommelier went down to the cellar and back up by the lift, and the bell rang at 22.17. The fibre and wine in the car match the waistcoat in his storage unit; the unit holds six years of forgery.

Over the sale. The château owes three million. My father said, ‘We’ll do this sale with Delorme and settle everything’; I didn’t want to do business with those Chicago men. At 22.00 I went up to my room; I passed my mother’s door.
He tugs at the sleeve of his jumper.
You argued with your father.

The victim’s wife.
I don’t discuss our family’s affairs.
In my room. Gaspard passed along the corridor at 22.00; I heard his voice. Thirty years with Henri… We slept in separate rooms, but I never went down to the cellar to him, I don’t.

The hand-operated lift from the cellar to the dining room:

· Car interior 70 × 60 × 90 cm. An adult of average build fits with knees drawn up; load limit 120 kg.

· On the cellar side, the car can also be hauled up from inside by pulling the rope with both hands.
· Arnaud Petit’s fingerprint on the inner handle of the hatch on the dining room side; the sommelier uses the lift every day.

THE CELLAR  /  SUSPICIOUS DEATH
At Fontainebleau, the owner of a château is found dead in his locked wine cellar on the night of a private sale. The key is in his pocket.

Antoine Brassard
66, wine expert; he was examining the bottles for the sale.
Yves Caron

Sommelier.
The cellar records aren’t with me, they’re with monsieur.
Serving cognac to the guests in the library. At 22.03 I passed along the corridor, the camera will have seen me; the cellar door was closed, monsieur was downstairs, I didn’t disturb him.
He turns his silver tastevin in his fingers.
Where were you between 22.00 and 22.30?
The lift? For twenty years that lift has carried only bottles. A person wouldn’t fit. I was in the corridor at 22.03.
Arnaud Petit — interview
Following the search.
No.
My prints are there every day. That proves nothing.

Six years. No one noticed, until that old expert sniffed the cork. After the cognac service I went down by the dining room lift; monsieur was pulling the bottles from the racks one by one. ‘Arnaud, what is this?’ he said. With the magnum in my hand… Then I squeezed into the car and pulled the rope. The door stayed locked the whole time; the key was in his pocket.
It was you who came up to the dining room by the lift at 22.17.
Arnaud Petit — second interview

The bell of the wine lift in the dining room wall rang at 22.17. It rings when the lift comes up from the cellar. I went; the car was empty. Monsieur sometimes sends up bottles; if he can’t… an empty car was strange. I didn’t tell anyone.
She folds the corner of her apron and smooths it.
Did you hear anything during the night?
Housekeeper.
I run the house; I don’t know the rest.
Rosa Pinto — interview
No one. The guests were in the library. Mr Arnaud wasn’t in the library for a while; I thought he’d gone down to the cellar for a bottle.
Who was in the dining room when the bell rang?

On the night of 8 June 2030, at a château near Fontainebleau, after a private sale of works, the château’s owner Henri de Vauclair (68) was found dead in his own wine cellar. A heavy head wound; beside him, a broken magnum.

The cellar’s only door was found locked; the key in the victim’s pocket. The door was opened at 23.40 with housekeeper Rosa Pinto’s spare key.

At the château that night: his wife Hélène, his son Gaspard, the sommelier Arnaud Petit, the housekeeper Rosa Pinto, the wine expert Yves Caron, the buyer’s representative from Chicago Marcus Doyle, and Antoine Brassard of Maison Delorme.
INCIDENT REPORT
Send the wine lift for examination
Request permission to search Arnaud Petit’s storage unit

A storage unit rented in Melun in Arnaud Petit’s name (with the branch chief’s approval):

· 214 blank, aged wine labels; great château vintages from 1945–1990. Boxes of old corks, tea and coffee dye.
· 86 genuine bottles taken from the château cellar; correspondence with a buyer in Luxembourg: ‘€1.4 million over six years’.
· A black wool waistcoat on a hanger; glass dust and red wine on the collar; its fibres match the fibre in the lift.
THE SOMMELIER’S STORAGE UNIT — SEARCH

The corridor camera showed the door never opened, the housekeeper the lift bell ringing at 22.17, and the lift examination the fibre and wine in the car. The storage search, opened on two grounds, gave the forgery and the waistcoat.
A locked room is locked only at the doors you know about. Ask about the route the person who runs the house uses every day.
Fontainebleau — June 2030

For six years the sommelier Arnaud Petit had been swapping the château’s great wines for fakes and selling the real ones. On the night of the private sale, when the expert Yves Caron found a 1961 to be fake, Henri de Vauclair went down to the cellar. Between cognac services, Petit went down by the wine lift in the dining room, killed his employer with a magnum as he pulled bottles from the racks, then squeezed into the car and hauled himself up by the rope. The door stayed locked throughout.
Who killed Henri de Vauclair?
